agentCan: Generate the exact CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION SQL snippet for each customer (your redirect URI, client type, token settings)
Implement the full authorization-code flow, token refresh, and per-account credential storage
Draft the customer-admin setup guide (SQL, secret retrieval, role decisions)

approval.trigger: No Snowflake-side review, approval, waitlist, or marketplace gate exists for OAuth connections. The integration object works the moment the customer's admin creates it. What gates connection is entirely customer-side: an ACCOUNTADMIN creating the integration, the user holding a consentable role, and network policies.

blockers.detail: There is no developer portal and no global app. Every customer account needs its own security integration, created by that account's ACCOUNTADMIN (or a CREATE INTEGRATION privilege holder), with its own client ID and secret pair. Your onboarding friction lives entirely on the customer's side, and your only lever is excellent setup documentation and ready-to-run SQL.
blockers.howToClear: Ship a copy-paste SQL snippet with your parameters filled in, plus a 5-minute admin guide. Expect the customer's internal change process, not the SQL, to dominate calendar time.
blockers.title: The customer must run SQL to create your 'app'

blockers.detail: ACCOUNTADMIN, ORGADMIN, GLOBALORGADMIN, and SECURITYADMIN are on the blocked list by default, so users cannot consent to admin roles out of the box. (The custom-clients guide says they cannot be removed and to contact Support; the SQL reference describes an account parameter for allowing them. Either way it is a deliberate customer-side act.)
blockers.howToClear: Design your tool around ordinary custom roles your customers create for it; never assume admin-role access.
blockers.title: Privileged roles are blocked by default

blockers.detail: Endpoints, integration names, and client credentials are all per-account. A multi-tenant tool must store and select the right credential set per customer account; there is no single client ID for your product.
blockers.howToClear: Model credentials per customer account from day one, including the two-secret rotation pair.
blockers.title: Credentials are per-account, not global

sources.label: Configure Snowflake OAuth for custom clients

tested: Read-only verification: integration flavors, required SQL parameters, role blocking, token lifetimes, consent behavior, and the absence of any review step were checked against current docs.snowflake.com pages (no account created, no SQL run)
unverified: No timelines exist to quote: the docs state no review periods or onboarding durations, and customer-admin turnaround is unquantifiable.
No documented path exists for becoming a named partner application (the Tableau/Looker list); how a vendor gets added is not described.
No prescribed pattern for how a SaaS vendor should receive and store per-account client secrets from customers.
MFA policy specifics for the Snowflake OAuth consent login are not spelled out in the pages read.
Minor doc tension: the guide says privileged roles 'cannot be removed' from the blocked list while the SQL reference describes an account parameter to allow them; both are reported, neither resolved.

alternatives: External OAuth (the customer's own IdP, Okta/Entra ID, is the authorization server; fits an enterprise's internal tool behind its own SSO, not a multi-tenant vendor)
Partner applications (a closed, Snowflake-defined list of BI tools like Tableau and Looker; no documented way for a new vendor to join)
flavor.recommended: Snowflake OAuth for custom clients: a 'security integration' (CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION ... TYPE = OAUTH, OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM), CONFIDENTIAL client type for a server-side tool
flavor.why: Snowflake itself is the authorization server, so the flow works against any customer's account with no dependency on their IdP. The catch: the 'app registration' is a SQL object inside each customer's account, not something you create once in a portal. There is even an IS_AGENTIC flag to mark sessions from your integration as agent sessions.

humanMust: The CUSTOMER's ACCOUNTADMIN runs the CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION SQL and retrieves the client secrets
The customer decides role allow/block lists, network policy, and refresh-token settings
The end user logs in and consents to a role in the browser (the docs explicitly say the authorize endpoint must be opened in an interactive browser, not via cURL)
Someone securely hands the per-account client ID/secret pair to your configuration
name: Snowflake
nuances: Access tokens are short: default 10 minutes, hard-capped at 1 hour. Refresh tokens for custom clients default to 90 days (range 1-90).

Single-use refresh token rotation is opt-in and unforgiving: if enabled, every refresh invalidates all previous tokens, and reusing an old one invalidates everything (intrusion detection by design). Persist the new refresh token after every refresh or connections break.
Consent is sticky and additive: re-authorizing only expands a user's consented role set; shrinking it requires ALTER USER ... REMOVE DELEGATED AUTHORIZATIONS.
Sessions are single-role by default; USE ROLE inside an OAuth session needs OAUTH_ANY_ROLE_MODE enabled plus the session:role-any scope.
Scopes are role-centric (session:role:<ROLE_NAME>), not data-centric like other providers; role names are case-sensitive.

PrivateLink wrinkle for hosted tools: the browser leg can use the PrivateLink URL, but your backend's token request cannot resolve a PrivateLink hostname, so the token endpoint must be a public Snowflake URL.
prerequisites: Your tool's OAuth redirect URI (TLS required) and chosen integration parameters (client type, token validities, PKCE enforcement)
A customer-facing SQL snippet and admin instructions (you cannot create anything in Snowflake yourself)
Per-customer-account credential storage in your backend

steps.detail: For a server-side SaaS/agent backend: Snowflake OAuth for custom clients, OAUTH_CLIENT_TYPE = 'CONFIDENTIAL' (PUBLIC + PKCE if your client ships to desktops). Snowflake offers an IS_AGENTIC parameter to mark sessions from your integration as agent sessions.
steps.title: Choose the custom-client flavor

steps.detail: Prepare the exact statement for customers: CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION with TYPE = OAUTH, OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM, your OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI (query parameters are not included in the registered value), plus your choices for refresh tokens, PKCE enforcement (OAUTH_ENFORCE_PKCE, recommended), allowed/blocked role lists, and token validities.
steps.title: Write the integration SQL for customers

steps.detail: Only an ACCOUNTADMIN (or CREATE INTEGRATION holder) in the customer's account can run it. This is the step that replaces 'registering your app': it happens per customer, inside their account, on their schedule.
steps.time: Minutes of SQL; calendar time is the customer's change process
steps.title: Customer admin creates the integration

steps.detail: The admin retrieves the pair with SYSTEM$SHOW_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRETS('<integration_name>'). Two secrets exist (OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET and _2) to support rotation without downtime. They must reach your configuration securely; Snowflake prescribes no hand-off pattern for SaaS vendors.
steps.title: Retrieve and hand off the client credentials

steps.detail: Endpoints are per-account: <account_url>/oauth/authorize and <account_url>/oauth/token-request. Send the user to authorize with client_id, response_type=code (the only supported type), redirect_uri, and scope (session:role:<ROLE> pins the role; refresh_token requests offline access). Exchange the code at the token endpoint via client_secret_basic/post or private_key_jwt.
steps.title: Implement the authorization-code flow

steps.detail: The user authenticates on Snowflake's own page and consents to a specific role (and to refresh-token access if requested). Consent persists and is additive across re-authorizations until explicitly revoked.
steps.title: User consents to a role

tagline: The portal-less provider: there is no app to register with Snowflake. Your 'OAuth app' is a SQL object the customer's own admin creates inside their account, one account at a time.

time.active: Developer: ~half a day (standard OAuth client + per-account credential handling + customer SQL docs). Customer admin: minutes of SQL per account
time.total: No waiting on Snowflake; real-world time is dominated by each customer's internal admin process
